wine.name: Schloss Johannisberger Riesling Grünlack Spätlese
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, Spätlese: late picked, at least 85 degrees Oechsle in the Rheingau
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, as the hill has been planted since 1720.
wine.sites: The estate's single vineyard in one piece on the hill below the schloss, facing south over the Rhine, on loess and loam over Taunus quartzite.
wine.making: Picked by hand in selective late passes, the grapes are pressed gently and fermented cool in the cellars under the schloss, and the fermentation is stopped to leave a gentle natural sweetness before the wine is bottled.
wine.glass: Ripe apple, white peach and quince over orange zest and wet stone; a gentle sweetness held by firm Rheingau acidity, with age bringing honey, toast and smoke.
wine.ageing: Pleasing young, it gains depth for ten to twenty years, and a strong vintage lasts for decades.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The green capsule of the estate's colour code, marking its Spätlese.
The estate's name standing for the village, as an Ortsteil, with no village before it.
Late picked, at least 85 degrees Oechsle in the Rheingau; the word the estate's legend of 1775 gave the language.

records.table: A green capsule marks Schloss Johannisberg's Grünlack Spätlese, Riesling from the hill where, as the estate tells it, the late harvest of 1775 gave Germany the word. Apple and peach over stone, it is gently sweet with a firm backbone.
records.story: The hill at Johannisberg took its first vines from Benedictine monks, who founded a monastery there around 1100. After the Thirty Years War left it ruined, the Prince-Abbots of Fulda took the estate, built the schloss and in 1720 planted the hill to Riesling alone. In 1775, so the story goes, the courier carrying the Prince-Abbot's leave to begin the harvest arrived weeks late; the grapes had shrivelled and rotted on the vine, the wine made from them was a revelation, and Spätlese, the late harvest, entered the language. The estate's chronology adds an Auslese in 1787 and an Eiswein in 1858. In 1816, after the Congress of Vienna, the Emperor Francis I of Austria (1768 to 1835) gave the schloss to his chancellor, Prince Klemens von Metternich (1773 to 1859), on condition that a tenth of each harvest went to the Habsburgs. The estate came to code its wines by the colour of the capsule, the Rotlack for Kabinett, the Grünlack for Spätlese and the Silberlack for its dry Grosses Gewächs, so a guest can read the style from across the room. Pour the Grünlack Spätlese with the legend, and tell it as the estate's claim rather than as proven history.

others.name: Schloss Johannisberger Riesling Rotlack Kabinett
others.note: The red capsule, the entry into the estate's colour code.

others.name: Schloss Johannisberger Riesling Silberlack Grosses Gewächs
others.note: The silver capsule, the estate's dry flagship from the same hill.

traps: Johannisberg here is a district of Geisenheim in the Rheingau; Johannisberg in the Swiss Valais is a name for Silvaner.
The Spätlese story of 1775 is the estate's claim, to be told as such rather than as proven history.
Johannisberger Erntebringer is a Grosslage over neighbouring villages, not Schloss Johannisberg.

cards.front: Schloss Johannisberg's capsules: which colour marks the Spätlese, and which the dry Grosses Gewächs?
cards.back: Grünlack, green, for the Spätlese; Silberlack, silver, for the dry Grosses Gewächs.

cards.front: What happened at Schloss Johannisberg in 1775, as the estate tells it?
cards.back: The courier bringing leave to pick came late; the rotted grapes made a celebrated wine, and Spätlese got its name.

wine.name: Kiedrich Gräfenberg Riesling Trockenbeerenauslese
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, Trockenbeerenauslese: shrivelled noble rot berries, at least 150 degrees Oechsle
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from berries shrivelled by noble rot.
wine.sites: The Gräfenberg, a steep slope set back from the river above Kiedrich, on phyllite and slate; mists from the Rhine in autumn bring the noble rot.
wine.making: Pickers go through the vineyard many times, taking shrivelled berries one by one. The thick, sticky juice ferments for months, very slowly, to a low alcohol with a great weight of natural sugar left behind.
wine.glass: Dried apricot, candied orange peel and saffron over acacia honey and caramelised pineapple; syrupy yet electric, its great sweetness carried by high acidity to a finish that seems to last for minutes.
wine.ageing: Already rich on release, it lives for half a century and more, slowly turning towards toffee, black tea and dried fig.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass and a small pour, alone or with a fruit tart.

label.means: The village and the vineyard; older labels read Kiedricher Gräfenberg.
Dried berry selection: shrivelled noble rot berries picked one by one, at least 150 degrees Oechsle.
The region on the Rhine's north bank between Wiesbaden and Rüdesheim.

records.table: Single shrivelled berries, picked one by one on the steep slate of the Gräfenberg above Kiedrich, make Robert Weil's Riesling Trockenbeerenauslese. Honeyed and syrupy, apricot and orange peel, yet bright with acidity, it is a dessert served in a small glass.
records.story: The estate began with a scholar. Its founder, a German who taught at the Sorbonne in Paris, left France after the war of 1870 and in 1875 bought his first vineyards at Kiedrich. In 1879 he bought the estate of an English baronet in the village, with its manor house and vines, and made it the family's home. As the house tells it, its sweet wines were poured at the imperial courts of Europe before the First World War, and the Gräfenberg, the steep slope behind the village, became the estate's signature. In 1988 the family sold a majority of the estate to the Japanese house of Suntory, and a great grandson of the founder ran it with the new capital behind him. From the 1990s the estate was known for making the whole botrytis ladder from the Gräfenberg, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese and Eiswein, year after year where others managed them only now and then, while making a dry Grosses Gewächs from the same slope. That steadiness made Weil the usual answer when a question asks for German sweet wine outside the Mosel. Against a Saar Trockenbeerenauslese the Rheingau's way with noble rot is plain to taste: the same grape in a fuller, firmer frame.

others.name: Kiedrich Gräfenberg Riesling Grosses Gewächs
others.note: The dry wine of the same slope, the estate's dry flagship.

others.name: Kiedrich Gräfenberg Riesling Auslese
others.note: Selected bunches with noble rot; gold capsule lots sit above the standard bottling.

others.name: Kiedrich Turmberg Riesling
others.note: A second Kiedrich slope the estate holds, bottled on its own.

traps: The Gräfenberg is at Kiedrich; do not place it at Erbach or Rüdesheim.
A Trockenbeerenauslese is sweet: trocken here means the dried berry, not a dry wine.
A Rheingau Trockenbeerenauslese needs the same 150 degrees Oechsle as the Mosel's, though the lower Prädikate ask more here.

cards.front: Robert Weil's Trockenbeerenauslese: what does trocken mean in the name?
cards.back: The dried, shrivelled berry, picked one by one; the wine itself is intensely sweet.

cards.front: On what rock does Robert Weil's Gräfenberg grow, and where?
cards.back: Phyllite and slate, on a steep slope set back from the river above Kiedrich.

questions.q: A guest sees Trockenbeerenauslese on Robert Weil's Kiedrich Gräfenberg and asks if it is a dry wine. What do you say?
opts: No: it is intensely sweet, from shrivelled noble rot berries
Yes: trocken means dry, so it is a dry Riesling
Yes: it is the estate's Grosses Gewächs by another name
No: it is a sparkling Sekt from late picked grapes
questions.exp: Trockenbeerenauslese means a selection of dried berries, shrivelled by noble rot, and the wine is intensely sweet; the dry wine of the Gräfenberg is the Grosses Gewächs.

As a banker in Frankfurt

wine.name: Schloss Vollrads Riesling Kabinett
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, Kabinett: the lightest Prädikat, at least 73 degrees Oechsle in the Rheingau
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, the grape of almost the whole estate.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyard in one piece around the moated tower above Winkel, on loess and loam, sloping gently south towards the Rhine.
wine.making: Picked by hand and pressed gently, the grapes ferment cool, mostly in stainless steel, as much of the Rheingau does. The Kabinett is made in more than one style, dry, off dry and fruity, and the label says which.
wine.glass: Green apple, lemon zest and white peach over wet stone, with a hint of fresh mint; light, crisp and restrained, the sweetness of the fruity style balanced by firm acidity.
wine.ageing: Fresh and easy young, it keeps and gains for ten years and more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, with river fish, asparagus or a light salad.

label.means: The estate's name alone, an Ortsteil, with no village or vineyard name before it.
The lightest Prädikat, at least 73 degrees Oechsle in the Rheingau.
Dry, or off dry; a Kabinett may be either, or fruity, so read the word.

records.table: Since 1211, by its own account, Schloss Vollrads has sold wine from the vineyard around its moated tower above Winkel. Its Riesling Kabinett is light and crisp, green apple and lemon over stone, and comes dry, off dry or fruity, which the label states in a word.
records.story: A sale of wine recorded in 1211 is where Schloss Vollrads begins its own history, and the estate counts it among the longest unbroken records of wine sales in the world. The moated tower at its heart was built in the fourteenth century by the Greiffenclau family, knights of the Rheingau, who held Vollrads for centuries and added the manor house beside it. The vineyard lies in one piece around the tower, and the label, since the estate is an Ortsteil, names the estate alone, with no village or vineyard before it. In 1984 the head of the family was among the founders of Charta, the growers' association that set out to bring dry Rheingau Riesling back to the table and led, in 1999, to the Erstes Gewächs law of Hesse. After his death in 1997 the family's centuries at Vollrads ended, and the estate passed to new owners who kept its name and its Riesling. The Kabinett is the estate's everyday voice and the clearest sign of its long habit of making one wine in several styles, dry, off dry and fruity. Its label is the lesson, an estate's name standing alone with the style written in a single word.

others.name: Schloss Vollrads Riesling Spätlese
others.note: The classical Rheingau reading of the Prädikat, riper and fuller than the Kabinett.

others.name: Schloss Vollrads Riesling Auslese

traps: The Greiffenclau family's centuries at Vollrads ended in the 1990s, so the family and the estate's later owners are two chapters.
Schloss Vollrads and Schloss Johannisberg are separate estates, both Ortsteile labelled without a village name.
A Vollrads Kabinett may be dry, off dry or fruity: the Prädikat sets ripeness at harvest, not sweetness in the glass.

wine.name: Rüdesheim Berg Schlossberg Riesling
wine.sites: The Berg Schlossberg, the steep heart of the Rüdesheimer Berg where the Rhine turns north, on slate and Taunus quartzite in terraces held by stone walls, facing south over the river.
wine.making: Picked by hand at full ripeness, the grapes ferment with their own yeasts, slowly, to dryness. The wine rests long on its lees before bottling and is labelled by village and vineyard alone, with no Prädikat.
wine.glass: Smoke, struck flint and wet slate over lime, yellow apple and blood orange; taut and bone dry, firm in grip and long, with a stony, faintly bitter edge at the finish.
wine.ageing: Tight for its first five to eight years, it then opens and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The castle hill of the Rüdesheimer Berg, the steep slope at the Rhine's bend.
The village, written before the vineyard; older labels read Rüdesheimer.
The grape; no Prädikat follows, since the estate labels by site alone and the wine is dry.

records.table: The label of Georg Breuer's Rüdesheim Berg Schlossberg Riesling names only the place, with no Prädikat, an argument the estate made before the Grosses Gewächs existed. Grown on steep slate and quartzite where the Rhine turns north, it is bone dry, smoky and taut.
records.story: Dry Riesling named for its vineyard is the idea that made the Breuer name. The family has made wine at Rüdesheim since the late nineteenth century, by its own account, and the estate takes its name from an earlier head of the family. In the 1970s and 1980s a son of the house led it towards one idea: that Rheingau Riesling should be dry, and should be named for the vineyard it came from rather than for its ripeness at harvest. In 1984 he was central to the founding of Charta, the growers' association that set a standard for dry Rheingau Riesling from good sites. The estate went further and dropped the Prädikat words from its labels altogether, naming its wines by village and vineyard alone, years before the state of Hesse wrote Erstes Gewächs into law in 1999 and before the VDP's Rheingau members moved to Grosses Gewächs with the 2012 vintage. He died in 2004, and his daughter took over the estate young and kept its course. The Berg Schlossberg, the steep slate and quartzite of the castle hill above the river, is the summit of the range. A place on the label and nothing else was the argument, and no wine of the estate makes it louder than the Berg Schlossberg.

others.name: Rauenthal Nonnenberg
others.note: A monopole at Rauenthal, broader and spicier than the Rüdesheim wines.

others.name: Rüdesheim Berg Rottland
others.note: The warmer of the Berg sites, rounder in fruit.

others.name: Rüdesheim Berg Roseneck

traps: The estate labels by site without a Prädikat, so the absence of Kabinett or Spätlese is a choice, not an omission.
Rüdesheim's Berg sites are slate and quartzite, unlike the loess and loam of the central Rheingau.
Rüdesheim Berg Schlossberg lies at the Rhine's bend in the Rheingau; Schlossberg is also an Alsace Grand Cru and a common vineyard name.

cards.front: Georg Breuer's Berg Schlossberg: on what rock, and where?

It is sweet; the Prädikat is printed on the capsule

questions.exp: Hesse recognised Erstes Gewächs in 1999; 1984 is Charta's founding, 2012 the VDP's move to Grosses Gewächs and 1971 the German wine law.

wine.name: Steinberger Riesling
wine.classification: An Ortsteil: a walled estate vineyard with the standing of a village
wine.sites: The Steinberg, the walled vineyard the Cistercian monks laid out on the slope above the abbey and Hattenheim, a gentle south facing hill closed by a stone wall and farmed as one block.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented cool, mostly in steel, the flagship Steinberger is made dry, in the state domaine's cellar beside the vineyard. Bottles of past vintages rest in the abbey's old Cabinet cellar, which the monks set aside for their reserve wines in 1712.
wine.glass: Yellow apple, quince and lemon peel over smoke and wet stone; dry, firm and broad in the Rheingau way, with a long, faintly salty finish.
wine.ageing: Firm young, it opens after three to five years and keeps for fifteen years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a white wine glass.

label.means: Wine of the Steinberg, an Ortsteil of Hattenheim, labelled without a village name.
The Cistercian abbey of 1136, whose name the state wine domaine carries.

records.table: Walled by the Cistercians of Kloster Eberbach in the Middle Ages and farmed as one block ever since, the Steinberg above Hattenheim gives Steinberger Riesling. Made dry, it is broad and firm, yellow apple and quince over smoke.
records.story: Cistercian monks sent from Clairvaux by Bernard of Clairvaux (1090 to 1153) founded the abbey of Eberbach in a wooded valley above Hattenheim in 1136. They cleared the slope below the forest and laid out the Steinberg in the twelfth century, and over the centuries they closed it with a stone wall, finished, by most accounts, in the eighteenth. The abbey grew into one of the large wine businesses of medieval Germany, sending its wine down the Rhine to the markets of Cologne. In 1712 the monks set aside a cellar, the Cabinet, for their reserve wines, and the word, as Kabinett, later came to name a Prädikat. When church lands were secularised in 1803 the abbey passed to the Duke of Nassau, with Nassau to Prussia in 1866, and after 1945 to the new state of Hesse, whose state wine domaine made the abbey and the Steinberg its home. Because the Steinberg is an Ortsteil, its wine is labelled Steinberger, with no village name, and it has stayed one block for some eight centuries in a country of divided vineyards. One wall, one vineyard, one name: eight centuries of monastic history stand behind the label.

others.name: Assmannshäuser Höllenberg Spätburgunder
others.note: The state domaine's red, from slate where the Rhine turns north, made in a cellar of its own.

others.name: Steinberger Riesling Auslese
others.note: The walled vineyard in a ripe year: selected bunches with noble rot.

traps: Steinberg is a vineyard, not a village; Steinberger on a label is an Ortsteil of Hattenheim.
Kloster Eberbach is the Cistercians' abbey and the state wine domaine; Schloss Johannisberg was the Benedictines' hill.
The word Kabinett comes from the abbey's Cabinet cellar of 1712, not from a classification of vineyards.

cards.front: Steinberger Riesling: who laid out the Steinberg, and how is it farmed?

A village beside Rüdesheim at the Rhine's bend
A Grosslage covering the slopes of Hattenheim
A district name for the whole Rheingau

For the refuter to confirm: the monks sent from Clairvaux, the wall finished in the eighteenth century (recalled as 1766), the wine shipped to Cologne, the secularisation of 1803, Nassau, Prussia in 1866 and Hesse after 1945, and the domaine's cellar beside the vineyard (recalled as opened in 2008, left out).
The plan names no style: the record teaches the dry Steinberger the domaine leads with; the soil of the Steinberg and the steel in the cellar are the author's recollection, and the soil is left out.
founded is 1136, the abbey's founding, which the Codex holds; the state domaine as such dates from after 1945.
